description:
We are a team of 4 friends, conformed by 3 devs and an artist. We are students from the Universidad Nacional de Villa Mercedes (UnViMe) and the Instituto de Formacion Docente Continua (IFDC).

Our challenge is Planet X and SPHEREx.
summary: OpenSPHEREx is a free web tool for exploring sky images from NASA’s SPHEREx mission and seeing how they change over time. Users enter sky coordinates or pick an example target. The tool shows that patch of sky as a short video, built from the telescope’s different passes and aligned so background stars stay still. That makes it easy to spot anything that moves or changes in brightness, such as asteroids, comets, brown dwarfs or variable stars. The viewer marks stars already cataloged by ESA’s Gaia mission, so users can tell what is known from what might be a new discovery. It is built for students, teachers and amateur astronomers with no formal scientific training. No coding is required, just a web browser.
details:
Project Details

What it does
OpenSPHEREx is a free web viewer that lets anyone see how the sky changes in images from NASA’s SPHEREx mission. Users type sky coordinates, pick one of the challenge targets (Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis) or open a shared link. The viewer then plays that patch of sky as a short animation across SPHEREx’s passes, which happen every six months. Stars that don’t move stay still, so anything that moves or changes brightness stands out: asteroids, comets, brown dwarfs, variable stars.

The viewer has three modes:

  • Blink: one stacked image per pass, played like a short video.
  • Frames: individual exposures over time.
  • Difference: a newer pass minus an older one. Anything that didn’t change turns gray, and a moving object shows up as a black and white pair.

Users can also pick any of SPHEREx’s six detector arrays or all of them combined, change the contrast stretch, and choose a background survey such as AllWISE. A Gaia DR3 overlay marks the stars that are already cataloged; their positions are corrected for proper motion to the date of each pass. A moving source with no Gaia marker is a candidate worth a closer look. For the challenge targets, an orange marker and an arrow show where the object will move over the next 10 years. The tool also measures the target’s brightness in every exposure and plots a spectrum and a light curve on demand.

How it works
The Python backend:

  • finds which SPHEREx frames cover a position using IRSA’s SIA v2 service;
  • reads only the needed pixel rows of each file directly from the public AWS S3 bucket using HTTP range requests, which cut a new region’s load from about 13 minutes to about 2.5 minutes, with the first image showing in about 20 seconds (IRSA’s cutout service is used as a fallback);
  • masks flagged pixels such as cosmic rays and hot pixels, and subtracts the zodiacal light model;
  • reprojects everything onto one fixed grid;
  • stacks the frames of each detector per pass, using the same contrast across the whole sequence so the background doesn’t flicker.

For saturated stars like R Draconis, brightness is measured in a ring around the saturated core, so the light curve still works. New SPHEREx data releases are detected automatically, and results are cached so repeated views load instantly.

Benefits and impact
Most known comets and brown dwarfs were found by volunteers comparing sky images. SPHEREx data is public but requires Python, FITS files and astronomy knowledge to use. OpenSPHEREx removes that barrier for students, teachers and amateur astronomers, who can explore new infrared data, and possibly contribute to discoveries, from a browser.

Built for non-scientists

  • Every control has a plain-language help bubble that explains what it does, what you will see and a tip. It works with mouse, keyboard, touch and screen readers.
  • A “What am I looking at?” caption describes what is on screen right now.
  • Guided tours walk first-time users through the coordinates screen and the viewer.
  • One-click recipes cover common tasks: spot something that moves, confirm the movement, look for cold objects, watch brightness change.
  • A searchable glossary is linked from the help bubbles.
  • The interface is available in 11 languages.

Tools

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Astropy, astroquery, PyVO, reproject, NumPy, Pillow, requests and pytest.
  • Frontend: React, Vite, React Router, Aladin Lite v3 (CDS) and Recharts.
  • Data: SPHEREx (NASA/IPAC IRSA and its public AWS S3 bucket), Gaia DR3 (ESA) and AllWISE.

Creativity
SPHEREx’s detectors observe a different wavelength at each position on the chip, so two raw frames from the same detector can look different even when nothing changed. Stacking each detector per pass gives images that can be compared fairly over time. We also turn the 102 bands into an on-demand spectrum. Every view can be shared or embedded through its URL, which includes the coordinates, field of view, detector, mode and language.

Factors we considered

  • Speed: IRSA is often overloaded, so we read from S3, retry downloads and validate every file before using it.
  • Hard targets: the challenge targets have very high proper motion, and some sit near the ecliptic pole, where SPHEREx observes almost continuously.
  • Accessibility: contrast and reduced-motion support.
  • Clear and honest: the tool never presents a candidate as a confirmed discovery.
